name: Cannabis / CBD for sleep

lead: Some people use cannabis or cannabidiol (CBD) to fall asleep more easily, aiming to wake up rested, recover better from training and look fresher around the skin and eyes.

The chain runs through faster sleep onset and more recovery. Wikipedia's CBD article says clinical evidence for a sleep benefit is limited and lists sleepiness as a common effect; only small trials exist, such as a 14-person phase 2 study of cannabinoids for insomnia in depression. CBD is the non-intoxicating constituent, while THC is the main intoxicating one.

paras: People take CBD as oils, gummies or capsules in the evening, or use cannabis products before bed, usually as part of a wind-down routine. Users describe the effect as a sense of calm and sleepiness within the hour; how long until sleep quality noticeably changes varies by person.

The FDA has cited possible liver toxicity, drug interactions, effects on mood and alertness, and unknown long-term effects. FDA studies found many CBD products were inaccurately labeled, and about half of 147 tested contained THC. Insomnia is listed among adverse effects of the approved CBD drug Epidiolex, which is indicated for seizure disorders rather than sleep. Legal status varies widely by country and state.

angle.text: Some users take cannabis or CBD to fall asleep faster, so they wake better rested and recover more from training, which shows up as fresher skin and eyes. Small clinical trials have looked at cannabinoids for insomnia.

lead: Cannabis products and cannabidiol (CBD) are used by some people to fall asleep more easily. In appearance terms the chain is sleep-based: people who sleep longer and more regularly say they look fresher, carry less under-eye darkness and recover better from training, so a product that helps them fall asleep is seen as supporting those looks goals indirectly.

CBD is a non-intoxicating cannabis constituent, while THC is the main intoxicating one. The only FDA-approved CBD medicine, Epidiolex (2018), is indicated for certain seizure disorders, not sleep.[1] Wikipedia notes that CBD may help with pain, sleep and addiction according to some claims, that clinical evidence is limited, and that somnolence is a common effect.[1]

Research on cannabis and sleep is mixed. A 2023 randomised crossover trial in adults with insomnia tested a medicinal cannabis oil against placebo and reported improved sleep, while a 2025 meta-analysis of polysomnography studies found cannabis does not consistently change sleep duration, latency or staging, and that withdrawal from regular use is associated with sleep disturbance.[2][3]
infobox: Varies; hemp-derived CBD with 0.3% THC or less is unscheduled federally in the US [1]
Mixed results in trials and meta-analyses [2][3]

paras: Users take cannabis by smoking, vaping or edibles, and CBD as oils, gummies or hemp flower, often in the evening.[4][5] On T Nation, one poster described using a high-CBD edible alongside a calming supplement and said it worked well for sleep, while another asked what CBD oil actually does and noted that it is heavily hyped.[4][5]

CBD side effects are dose-related and include somnolence, sedation, fatigue, diarrhea and appetite changes [1]. The FDA has raised concerns about liver toxicity, interactions with prescription drugs, gastrointestinal problems and effects on alertness and mood, and in later updates about long-term effects, pregnancy and male fertility [1].
Product quality studies found labeling problems: a 2017 analysis of online US products found 69% mislabeled, and a 2020 FDA study of 147 products found half contained THC [1].
A 2024 review of cannabis harms in the Annual Review of Medicine covers health risks of use more broadly.[6]

A 2023 double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of a medicinal cannabis oil in 29 adults with self-reported insomnia reported improved sleep over six weeks, as indicated by its title.[2] A 2025 systematic review and meta-analysis of 18 polysomnography studies (nine in the meta-analysis) found no consistent change in sleep duration, latency, wake time, efficiency or stages with cannabis administration, noted that early REM-suppression findings came from small high-THC studies, and found withdrawal consistently associated with shorter sleep and longer sleep onset.[3]
A phase 2 trial of cannabinoids for insomnia in major depression (n=14) was completed in 2023; no results are reported in its registry entry.[7]

lore.intro: On looksmax.org and T Nation, cannabis and CBD come up as sleep aids and as part of broader questions about how substance use affects looks and health.[4][5][8]
